summary:
Find Earth Terrain Analogs for the Moon and Mars
Earth is our most accessible natural laboratory for preparing future lunar and Martian exploration missions. Certain environments on Earth, such as the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, and Death Valley, share specific geological and environmental characteristics with the Moon and Mars, making them valuable analog sites for scientific research, equipment testing, and mission preparation.
Our project aims to develop a web-based platform that identifies and analyzes potential Earth locations with characteristics analogous to the lunar and Martian environments. By combining relevant geographical, geological, and environmental datasets, the platform helps identify suitable locations, evaluate their similarities and differences, and explore their potential applications in space exploration research.
The results are presented through interactive maps and visualizations, allowing users to explore candidate locations and understand why each environment may serve as an analog for specific lunar or Martian conditions.
Rather than assuming that any Earth location perfectly replicates another planetary environment, our platform focuses on identifying meaningful similarities, highlighting environmental differences, and supporting the selection of terrestrial sites for future space exploration research and mission preparation

Terrain Analogs — Data Sources, Tools & Open-Source Materials

Data Sources

The Terrain Analogs project relies on several open-access geospatial and planetary datasets. The primary source is NASADEM_HGT V001, provided by NASA, which supplies Earth elevation data for the three original benchmark locations and the regional scan of 1,176 terrain patches across Wadi Rum, Ramon, and Harrat Khaybar. These elevation datasets are used to extract terrain features and generate route grids.

The project also uses LRO/LOLA data (Site04 and Site01) from NASA to obtain elevation information for the Shackleton Rim and Connecting Ridge reference locations on the Moon. In addition, MRO/CTX elevation data, distributed by the United States Geological Survey (USGS), are used for two reference patches within Jezero Crater on Mars: Jezero Landing Area and Western Jezero. The exact elevation product remains to be confirmed.

Furthermore, Copernicus DEM GLO-30, provided through the Copernicus Programme and the European Space Agency (ESA), is used for the Wadi Qelt benchmark and for a matched-footprint elevation source comparison at Wadi Rum. ESA WorldCover 2021 is also available as an optional land-cover screening dataset, particularly for identifying bare or sparsely vegetated areas (Class 60). This screening is kept separate from the planetary terrain similarity score.

Data Sources and Access Links

The main data sources can be accessed through their official platforms. NASADEM HGT V001 is available at https://lpdaac.usgs.gov/products/nasadem_hgtv001/. The Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) LOLA datasets are accessible through the PDS Geosciences Node at https://pds-geosciences.wustl.edu/missions/lro/lola.htm. Mars CTX data and related planetary resources are available through USGS Astrogeology at https://astrogeology.usgs.gov/. Copernicus DEM data can be accessed through https://dataspace.copernicus.eu/, while ESA WorldCover datasets are available at https://esa-worldcover.org/.

All links require final verification, and some exact product identifiers and direct dataset URLs, particularly for the lunar and Martian elevation references, remain to be confirmed.

Tools and Technologies

The project was developed using Python for data-processing scripts and GDAL for raster reading, reprojection, and slope derivation. NumPy was used to calculate terrain characteristics, including median slope, the percentage of area with slopes below 10 degrees, and relative relief measured as the difference between the 95th and 5th percentiles (P95–P5).

JavaScript powers the in-browser ranking system, interactive features, and route-connectivity simulation. Leaflet is used to build the interactive project map. For geospatial data exchange, the project uses GeoTIFF for raster datasets and GeoJSON for vector data, including terrain patch boundaries.

Methodology

The project does not use machine-learning model training or vector databases. Instead, it implements an exact feature-vector similarity search using a normalized, weighted Manhattan distance metric.

The similarity calculation uses three normalization scales: 5 degrees for slope, 15 percentage points for the proportion of terrain with slopes below 10 degrees, and 100 meters for relative relief. These measurements allow the system to rank Earth locations according to how closely their terrain characteristics match selected lunar and Martian reference sites.

Open-Source Materials

The project uses several open-source software libraries and tools. These include GDAL, available at https://gdal.org/; NumPy, available at https://numpy.org/; and Leaflet, available at https://leafletjs.com/.

The exact software versions and applicable licenses are still to be confirmed. The project's source-code repository and complete data bundle links also remain to be provided.

Disclaimer

This project is an independent submission to the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or officially supported by NASA.
